rows.syllabus_topic: Basic Concepts — permissible delegation of administrative implementation
rows.title: Delegation Guided by a Complete Law and Sufficient Standard
rows.prompt: Congress enacted a law making battery producers bear collection costs, identifying the covered products and liable persons, and directing an environmental board to compute an annual charge from collection volume, audited disposal cost, and toxicity weights fixed in the statute. After notice and hearing, the board calculated the charge using only those factors. VoltWorks argues that Congress had to state the final peso amount itself. Did Congress unconstitutionally delegate legislative power to the environmental board?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Congress made the law and confined the board to calculating its charge under legislatively fixed standards.

Legal Basis: Delegation to an administrative agency is valid when the statute is complete in its essential terms and supplies a sufficient standard that guides and limits implementation. Congress must determine policy and legal consequences, but it may authorize an agency to ascertain facts, apply technical formulas, and fill in operational details.

Application: The statute selected the regulated products and liable producers, imposed the cost obligation, and prescribed measurable volume, disposal-cost, and toxicity variables. The board could not choose a different policy or subject; it merely calculated the amount from the formula after the required hearing.

Conclusion: Hence, the board exercised permissible administrative implementation rather than delegated lawmaking power.

rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights — zones of privacy and social-media settings
rows.title: Reasonable Expectation of Privacy in a Public Social-Media Post
rows.prompt: Rina uploaded a video to an unrestricted social-media account that anyone could view, download, and share. A classmate sent the public link to the school discipline office, which viewed only that post without bypassing a password, opening a private message, or obtaining hidden account data. Rina claims that the constitutional right to privacy barred school officials from viewing the post without her consent. Does the privacy guarantee protect Rina's deliberately public post from ordinary viewing?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Rina did not retain a reasonable expectation of privacy in content she deliberately exposed to unrestricted public viewing.

Legal Basis: Constitutional privacy protects an expectation that the person actually manifested and that society is prepared to recognize as reasonable. Under Vivares v. St. Theresa's College, social-media privacy depends materially on the user's chosen settings and voluntary disclosure; content knowingly made public is ordinarily outside that protected expectation.

Application: Rina selected an unrestricted account and permitted every internet user to view, copy, and share the video. The school used the same public link available to everyone and did not penetrate any private communication or restricted portion of her account.

Conclusion: Hence, the privacy guarantee did not prevent ordinary viewing of Rina's deliberately public post.

rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights — requisites of a valid classification
rows.title: Equal Protection and Full-Fleet Zero-Emission Classification
rows.prompt: To reduce urban emissions, a city ordinance grants a five-year registration-fee rebate to public-transport operators whose entire active fleet uses zero-emission vehicles. Transport data show materially greater air-quality gains from full-fleet conversion. Every operator may qualify at any time during the transition, and every qualifying operator receives the same rebate. A diesel-bus operator challenges the classification because both groups carry passengers. Does the full-fleet classification satisfy the requirements of equal protection?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The classification rests on a substantial and relevant distinction and operates equally and prospectively within the defined class.

Legal Basis: Equal protection permits classification when it rests on substantial distinctions, is germane to the law's purpose, is not confined to existing conditions, and applies equally to every member of the class. Persons differently situated in a way material to the legislative objective need not receive identical treatment.

Application: Full-fleet conversion produces demonstrably greater emissions reduction, making the distinction relevant to air quality. The five-year window allows any operator to enter the class, and the ordinance grants the same rebate to every operator meeting the objective zero-emission condition.

Conclusion: Thus, the full-fleet classification satisfies equal protection because it substantially advances emissions reduction, remains open to every operator during the transition, and treats all qualifying operators alike.

rows.syllabus_topic: Executive Department — factual basis for martial law
rows.title: Rebellion Without Complete Territorial Control
rows.prompt: An armed organization seized three municipal halls, burned police stations, freed detainees, and announced that it was replacing national authority across the province. Intelligence reports showed coordinated attacks on power facilities and the flight of local officials. The President proclaimed martial law in the province for sixty days and reported to Congress within forty-eight hours. The challengers concede these facts but argue that the rebels had not gained complete control of the province. Must rebels first obtain complete territorial control before the President may proclaim martial law?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Complete rebel control of territory is not a constitutional prerequisite to a martial-law proclamation.

Legal Basis: Article VII, Section 18 permits the President to proclaim martial law for not more than sixty days when actual invasion or rebellion exists and public safety requires it. Judicial review examines the factual sufficiency of those two predicates; the Constitution does not require that insurgents first succeed in governing or controlling the whole affected territory.

Application: Seizure of government buildings, attacks on police and infrastructure, release of detainees, displacement of officials, and an announced effort to replace lawful authority objectively indicate actual rebellion and a public-safety danger. The rebels' failure to control every part of the province does not negate those facts.

Conclusion: Thus, the proclamation is not invalid for lack of complete territorial control because actual rebellion and the needs of public safety—not successful rebel governance—are the constitutional predicates.

rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Commissions — Civil Service Commission jurisdiction and merit-system integrity
rows.title: CSC Discipline for Civil-Service Examination Impersonation
rows.prompt: A police applicant arranges for another person to take a promotional examination in his name. He argues that Republic Act No. 8551 transferred police-examination administration to NAPOLCOM and therefore removed all CSC authority over the fraud. Did that transfer divest the CSC of disciplinary jurisdiction over the civil-service examination anomaly?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The transfer did not remove the CSC's disciplinary authority over civil-service examination fraud.

Legal Basis: Article IX-B makes the CSC the central personnel agency. San Felix v. Civil Service Commission holds that Republic Act No. 8551 did not completely divest the CSC of jurisdiction over anomalies and irregularities in civil-service examinations.

Application: NAPOLCOM may administer the police examination, but impersonation and dishonesty remain civil-service offenses within the CSC's constitutional personnel jurisdiction.

Conclusion: Thus, the CSC may investigate and discipline the applicant for the examination fraud.

rows.syllabus_topic: Legislative Department — duly published rules for inquiries in aid of legislation
rows.title: Legislative Inquiry Conducted Without Duly Published Rules
rows.prompt: A Senate committee summoned Lina to an inquiry during a new Congress. The committee's prior rules of procedure had not been published for that Congress, and replacement rules were uploaded only after Lina appeared. Acting under the unpublished rules, the committee cited her in contempt and ordered her detained for refusing to answer. Is the contempt detention valid despite the absence of duly published governing rules when the hearing occurred?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Legislative contempt cannot rest on an inquiry conducted without the duly published rules required by the Constitution.

Legal Basis: Article VI, Section 21 permits each House or its committees to conduct inquiries in aid of legislation only in accordance with duly published rules of procedure. Publication gives witnesses authoritative notice of the procedure governing compulsory attendance and contempt; rules published only after the hearing cannot retroactively validate coercive action already taken.

Application: Lina appeared when no governing inquiry rules for the Congress had been duly published, yet the committee invoked those unavailable procedures to detain her. Uploading replacement rules only after her appearance supplied no prior notice and could not cure the constitutional defect.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the contempt order and resulting detention are invalid for want of duly published rules.

rows.syllabus_topic: Constitutional Rights — writ of amparo
rows.title: Amparo Relief for a Concrete Threat of Enforced Disappearance
rows.prompt: After organizer Lia criticized a security operation, uniformed personnel repeatedly visited her home, photographed her family, and told neighbors that she would disappear. An official social-media page displayed her photograph beside an armed-group emblem. Lia preserved the posts and presented sworn witnesses to the visits and threats. She remains physically free but alleges an imminent State-linked threat of enforced disappearance. May Lia seek a writ of amparo before an actual abduction occurs?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Amparo may protect against a substantially proven threat of enforced disappearance before the threatened abduction is completed.

Legal Basis: The Rule on the Writ of Amparo covers unlawful acts or omissions of public officials or private persons that violate or threaten life, liberty, or security in connection with an extralegal killing or enforced disappearance. The petitioner must establish the covered violation or threat by substantial evidence, but need not await consummation of the feared harm.

Application: Uniformed visits, surveillance of Lia's family, an express warning that she would disappear, and official online branding tied the danger to State actors and to enforced disappearance. Her preserved posts and sworn witnesses provide concrete evidence beyond an unparticularized fear.

Conclusion: Hence, Lia may seek amparo before an actual abduction occurs because substantial evidence shows a State-linked threat of enforced disappearance.

rows.title: Presidential Communications Privilege for Solicited Advice
rows.prompt: The President asked the Energy Secretary for confidential advice on a proposed cross-border power agreement. The Secretary sent a private memorandum evaluating negotiation options, national-security risks, and possible presidential responses. During a legislative inquiry, the Executive Secretary, expressly acting by presidential authority, identified that memorandum and specifically invoked presidential communications privilege. The committee showed no particularized overriding need for it. Is the memorandum presumptively protected by presidential communications privilege?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The solicited and confidential advice concerns a presidential decision and falls within the qualified presumption of privilege.

Legal Basis: Presidential communications privilege presumptively protects confidential communications authored or solicited by the President or close operational advisers in shaping a presidential decision. The privilege must be specifically invoked by presidential authority and is qualified, so it may yield upon a demonstrated sufficiently compelling and particularized need for the information.

Application: The President personally requested the memorandum, and its negotiation and national-security analysis was prepared to guide his decision on an international power agreement. The authorized invocation identified the exact communication and basis, while the committee offered no overriding particularized need to defeat the presumption.

Conclusion: Hence, the memorandum is presumptively protected because the President solicited confidential advice from a Cabinet adviser on a foreign-relations decision, the privilege was specifically invoked by presidential authority, and the committee showed no overriding particularized need.

rows.syllabus_topic: National Territory — Maritime zones and coastal-State enforcement against marine dumping
rows.title: Coastal-State Enforcement Against Dumping in the EEZ
rows.prompt: A foreign vessel is caught dumping toxic hospital waste twenty nautical miles from Palawan. Its officers argue that the Philippines has no enforcement authority merely because the ship was beyond the twelve-nautical-mile territorial sea. Does that location alone immunize the dumping from lawful Philippine enforcement?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The location alone does not immunize dumping within the Philippine exclusive economic zone.

Legal Basis: UNCLOS Articles 210(5) and 216(1)(a) recognize the coastal State's right to permit, regulate, control, and enforce applicable laws against dumping within its territorial sea, exclusive economic zone, or continental shelf. Article 33 is not the source of punishment for dumping at twenty nautical miles; enforcement must rest on UNCLOS Part XII, applicable international standards, and Philippine implementing law.

Application: Twenty nautical miles is beyond the territorial sea but remains within the Philippine exclusive economic zone. Philippine authorities may therefore enforce valid anti-dumping measures under the Part XII framework, although they must identify and comply with the applicable domestic law and UNCLOS safeguards rather than rely on contiguous-zone jurisdiction alone.

Conclusion: Thus, the vessel's position beyond twelve nautical miles does not by itself defeat lawful Philippine enforcement against the dumping.

Article 33 is not the source of punishment for dumping at twenty nautical miles; enforcement must rest on UNCLOS Part XII, applicable international standards, and Philippine implementing law.
rows.controlling_doctrine: Dumping within a coastal State's exclusive economic zone is governed by UNCLOS Part XII: the coastal State may regulate and enforce applicable anti-dumping laws there, but Article 33 alone is not a general grant of criminal jurisdiction over environmental offenses.

rows.syllabus_topic: Judicial Department — actual case or controversy
rows.title: Ripeness of a Constitutional Challenge to a Pending Bill
rows.prompt: A technology association asks the Supreme Court to invalidate a bill requiring licenses for artificial-intelligence auditors. The House approved one version, a Senate committee is considering another, and no final measure has been enacted or presented to the President. No association member has received a license denial, penalty, or compliance order. Is there an actual and ripe case or controversy for judicial review?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The petition asks for an advisory opinion about a contingent proposal rather than an enforceable legal dispute.

Legal Basis: Judicial review under Article VIII requires an actual case or controversy involving concrete, opposing legal claims and an existing or imminent injury susceptible of judicial resolution. A challenge is unripe when it depends on uncertain future legislative events, and public importance cannot authorize an advisory opinion on a bill.

Application: The two chambers had not agreed on statutory text, the President had not acted, and no government officer had enforced any obligation against a member. Both the eventual law and any injury therefore depended on political events that might never occur.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the Court must dismiss the petition for want of an actual and ripe controversy because the challenged measure remains an unenacted bill and no association member faces an existing or imminent injury.

rows.syllabus_topic: Citizenship — Naturalization of refugees and reciprocity
rows.title: Naturalization of a Recognized Refugee Without Reciprocity
rows.prompt: Nadir, a recognized refugee, has lived in the Philippines for twelve years and possesses every statutory qualification for naturalization. His country of origin does not grant reciprocal naturalization rights to Filipinos. Does the absence of reciprocity automatically bar Nadir's petition?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Reciprocity does not automatically bar a qualified recognized refugee.

Legal Basis: The 1951 Refugee Convention and the Rule on Facilitated Naturalization of Refugees and Stateless Persons remove reciprocity as an obstacle for qualified refugees. Republic v. Karbasi applied the refugee framework in naturalization.

Application: Nadir is a recognized refugee and has been found otherwise qualified. Requiring reciprocity from the State from which he fled would defeat the facilitated protective framework.

rows.title: Regalian Doctrine and Unclassified Reclaimed Land
rows.prompt: A private developer reclaims part of Manila Bay under a service contract, then claims ownership by long possession even though no law or presidential act classified the reclaimed area as alienable land of the public domain. May the developer acquire ownership by prescription?

rows.title: Domestic Effect of a Nonbinding International Recommendation
rows.prompt: An international health conference adopted a nonbinding recommendation encouraging States to prohibit advertising of high-sugar food. The Philippines voted for it, but no treaty was concluded, Congress enacted no prohibition, and the Food Bureau identified no generally accepted customary rule imposing one. Does the nonbinding recommendation alone supply enforceable domestic authority for the order?

Answer: No. A nonbinding international recommendation does not by itself create an enforceable prohibition in Philippine law.

Application: The conference deliberately issued a recommendation rather than a treaty, Congress enacted no implementing prohibition, and the Bureau identified no customary international norm. Conclusion: Thus, the Bureau cannot enforce the advertising order solely on the basis of the nonbinding recommendation.

rows.title: State Immunity in a Contract Serving a Sovereign Function
rows.prompt: The Department of External Relations contracted with Harborstone Builders to repair an official diplomatic residence used in conducting foreign relations. The agreement contained no waiver of immunity, and Harborstone identified no statute consenting to suit. When the Department withheld final payment over structural defects, Harborstone sued the Republic directly and argued that every government contract automatically implies consent. Is the suit maintainable merely because the claim arose from a contract?

Answer: No. A contract connected with a sovereign function does not by itself constitute the State's consent to be sued.

Legal Basis: Article XVI, Section 3 declares that the State may not be sued without its consent. Application: Repair of an official diplomatic residence directly supported the Department's foreign-relations function rather than an ordinary profit-making venture. The contract contained no waiver, no law authorized the action, and the Republic timely invoked immunity instead of seeking affirmative judicial relief.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the direct suit against the Republic is not maintainable because repairing an official diplomatic residence served a sovereign function and neither law nor contract waived State immunity.

rows.title: Administrative Due Process Through Written Submissions
rows.prompt: A bank received an administrative charge for inaccurate regulatory reports, the supporting audit worksheets, and thirty days to file a verified answer with an expert report. The governing rules permit written adjudication and a motion for reconsideration. The bank deliberately submits nothing and later claims denial of due process because the agency held no trial-like hearing with live witnesses. Did the agency provide the bank the hearing required by administrative due process?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Notice and genuine opportunities for written explanation and reconsideration satisfied the administrative hearing requirement.

Legal Basis: Administrative due process requires notice of the charge and evidence and a meaningful opportunity to explain, support, and defend one's position before an impartial decision. Application: The bank knew the precise charge, received the audit material, and had thirty days to answer with expert evidence, followed by reconsideration. Its deliberate choice not to use either available procedure did not convert adequate opportunities to be heard into a constitutional denial.

Conclusion: Thus, the agency afforded administrative due process because the bank received the charge and supporting evidence and had meaningful opportunities to answer in writing and seek reconsideration.

rows.title: Presidential Supervision Cannot Replace Lawful Local Discretion
rows.prompt: A province lawfully chooses community clinics as the priority for its discretionary local development fund. Conclusion: Thus, the directive exceeds general supervision and intrudes on protected local autonomy.

rows.syllabus_topic: Business Organizations — director self-dealing under Section 31
rows.title: Voidability of an Unratified Self-Dealing Contract
rows.prompt: Luis operated Harbor Supplies as his sole proprietorship and also served as a director of Bayline Corporation. His presence was necessary for Bayline's quorum, his vote was necessary to approve a supply contract between Bayline and his sole proprietorship, and he did not disclose that personal interest. The contract price was thirty-five percent above independent quotations. No stockholder ratification occurred. Is the self-dealing contract valid against Bayline merely because its board approved it?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Board approval did not protect an undisclosed and unfair self-dealing contract for which Luis supplied the necessary quorum and vote.

Legal Basis: Section 31 of the Revised Corporation Code makes a director's contract with the corporation voidable unless the interested director's presence is unnecessary for quorum, the vote is unnecessary for approval, and the contract is fair and reasonable. Defects may be cured only by informed ratification representing at least two-thirds of outstanding capital stock, with full disclosure and substantive fairness.

Application: Luis was Bayline's director and the contracting seller through his sole proprietorship, concealed that personal interest, and provided both the quorum and decisive vote for a contract priced far above independent offers. Because the transaction was unfair and no informed two-thirds stockholder ratification occurred, none of the statutory protections validated it.

Conclusion: Thus, Bayline may avoid the self-dealing contract because Luis supplied the necessary quorum and vote, concealed his personal interest, approved an unfair price, and obtained no informed stockholder ratification.

rows.title: Zero-Rated Export Sale Does Not Alone Prove a VAT Refund
rows.prompt: A VAT-registered exporter proves that its output sale is zero-rated, but purchase invoices offered for the related input-tax refund omit essential VAT information required by the post-April 2024 invoicing rules. Is zero-rated status alone sufficient to establish the refund?

rows.title: Administrative Issuance Cannot Create a Franchise Tax
rows.prompt: Before Republic Act No. 11590, an offshore POGO licensee operated its gaming website abroad, accepted only foreign players abroad, and placed and paid all wagers abroad. The BIR nevertheless relied on Revenue Memorandum Circular No. 102-2017 to impose a five-percent franchise tax. At that time, no statute imposed that tax on offshore POGO licensees; the circular purported to derive it from general licensing rules. Could the BIR validly create and collect the franchise tax through the revenue circular?

Answer: No. A revenue circular cannot create a tax that Congress had not imposed by statute.

Legal Basis: The power to impose a tax is legislative, and every tax must rest on a clear statutory grant. The circular therefore did not merely explain a legislated liability; it attempted to make the foreign operator a taxable subject through administrative action alone.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the BIR could not validly impose the franchise tax through the circular before Republic Act No. 11590.

rows.title: Local Road-Impact Charge on Petroleum Products
rows.prompt: A municipality imposes a road-impact charge measured solely by every liter of petroleum delivered within its territory, whether or not municipal roads are used. Is the ordinance valid merely because the exaction is labeled a charge rather than a tax on petroleum products?

rows.title: Liability of a Purported Partner by Estoppel

rows.title: Piercing the Corporate Veil to Defeat Fraudulent Evasion
rows.prompt: Northbay Foods lost a final labor judgment. The next day, its sole shareholder formed Cedar Kitchens, transferred all Northbay equipment to Cedar without consideration, continued the same premises, managers, workers, customers, and bank signatories, and left Northbay assetless. rows.title: Material Concealment Unrelated to the Cause of Death
rows.prompt: When applying for life insurance, Ruben was asked whether a physician had diagnosed a heart condition during the previous five years. Six months earlier, his cardiologist had diagnosed serious arrhythmia requiring treatment, but Ruben intentionally answered no. The insurer proves that disclosure would have changed its underwriting terms. Ruben died from an unrelated accident within the contestable period, and the insurer timely sought rescission. May the insurer rescind for concealment although the undisclosed condition did not cause Ruben's death?

Legal Basis: Concealment is the neglect to communicate a material fact known to the insured that the insurer has no means of ascertaining. The insurer established that truthful disclosure would have changed its terms, and it invoked rescission within the contestable period; the accidental cause of death does not erase that material influence.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the insurer may timely rescind the policy for Ruben's material concealment.

rows.syllabus_topic: Special Commercial Laws — legal recognition and admissibility of electronic documents
rows.title: No Exclusion Solely for Electronic Form
rows.prompt: Aster Components sues on a supply agreement negotiated through company email. It offers the native message files, server logs showing that the records remained unaltered, and records-custodian testimony authenticating the messages and confirming their accessibility for later reference. The buyer objects only that no paper original exists. May the court exclude the authenticated agreement solely because it is electronic and has no paper counterpart?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Electronic form and the absence of a paper counterpart are not independent grounds for denying legal effect or admissibility.

Legal Basis: Sections 6, 7, and 12 of the Electronic Commerce Act recognize electronic data messages and documents and prohibit exclusion solely because of electronic form. An electronic record may satisfy writing and original requirements when it is accessible for later reference and its integrity and reliability are shown, while ordinary evidentiary rules still require competent authentication.

Application: Aster did not rely on an unexplained printout; it produced native messages, preservation logs, and custodian testimony showing accessibility, integrity, and authenticity. Because the buyer's sole objection is the missing paper original, that objection attacks electronic form rather than any unproved statutory safeguard.

Conclusion: Thus, the court may not exclude the authenticated agreement solely for lacking a paper counterpart.

rows.syllabus_topic: Banking — secrecy of deposits and statutory exceptions
rows.title: Narrow Scope of the Bank-Secrecy Subject-Matter Exception
rows.prompt: A company charged its cashier with taking business collections and asked the criminal court to disclose every transaction in her savings account for ten years. The Information alleged theft of company cash but asserted no ownership of the savings account or of its entire balance. The company argued that the records might help trace the missing collections and therefore made all deposited money the subject matter of litigation. Does the subject-matter exception in Republic Act No. 1405 authorize the requested disclosure?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Possible evidentiary usefulness does not make the cashier's entire protected deposit the subject matter of the criminal case.

Legal Basis: Republic Act No. 1405 makes Philippine-currency bank deposits confidential, subject only to strictly construed statutory exceptions. Deposited money is the subject matter of litigation when the action directly contests title, entitlement, or liability concerning that deposit itself; an account is not opened merely because its transactions may be relevant evidence of a different alleged wrong.

Application: The Information accused the cashier of taking company collections but did not claim the whole savings account or litigate legal rights in its balance. A decade-wide disclosure would reach transactions before and after the alleged theft solely because they might provide evidence, which is insufficient under the narrow exception.

Conclusion: Wherefore, Republic Act No. 1405 does not authorize disclosure because the criminal case concerns theft of collections, not title, entitlement, or liability concerning the savings deposit itself.

rows.title: Maximum Duration of an AMLA Freeze Order
rows.prompt: AMLC obtained a freeze order over Yambao's assets upon probable cause that he held property as a nominee for a retired general. The order remained effective for years even after the Republic filed a forfeiture case in which the trial court could issue an asset-preservation order. AMLC did not file, before expiration of the ordinary extension, a motion explaining any compelling need for a further freeze. May the freeze order remain effective indefinitely while the forfeiture case is pending?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. A freeze order is an interim remedy and cannot continue indefinitely in place of preservation relief in the forfeiture action.

Legal Basis: A freeze order under the Anti-Money Laundering Act is extraordinary, preemptive, and provisional. Under Yambao v. Application: The Republic had already commenced forfeiture litigation capable of preserving Yambao's assets, yet the separate freeze continued for years. Because AMLC filed no timely motion giving a compelling reason for additional duration, the interim order had exhausted its lawful preservatory function.

Conclusion: Thus, the indefinite freeze must be lifted without prejudice to a valid preservation order in the forfeiture case.

rows.title: Unfair Competition Through Deceptive Passing Off
rows.prompt: Elarfoods had long sold lechon under ELAR'S branding with a distinctive roasted-pig-on-bamboo-tray presentation and had built public goodwill around that business identity. Former employees formed Emzee Foods and marketed competing lechon using ELARZ wording and a closely imitated presentation, causing customers to believe that Emzee was an Elarfoods branch or franchise. The former employees knew that no affiliation existed. Did Emzee commit unfair competition by passing off its business as connected with Elarfoods?

Legal Basis: Section 168 of the Intellectual Property Code protects a person who has established goodwill in goods, business, or services against another's employment of deception or other means calculated to pass off competing goods or business as those of the first person. Emzee's founders knew the original business from their former employment, closely copied its wording and trade presentation, and thereby caused customers to perceive a nonexistent branch or franchise relationship.

Conclusion: Thus, Emzee is liable for unfair competition through deceptive passing off.

rows.syllabus_topic: Special Commercial Laws — effects of a rehabilitation commencement order
rows.title: Stay of Execution After a Rehabilitation Commencement Order
rows.prompt: A rehabilitation court issued and published a commencement order for Meridian Fabricators. Despite notice, a machinery supplier continued a collection case filed before rehabilitation, obtained a writ, and directed the sheriff to levy Meridian's production line. The supplier identified no statutory exception and argued only that its earlier filing allowed execution to finish. May the supplier continue levy and execution after the commencement order?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The commencement order stays enforcement and execution against the debtor regardless of the collection case's earlier filing.

Legal Basis: Section 16 of the Financial Rehabilitation and Insolvency Act stays all actions or proceedings to enforce claims against the debtor and suspends execution, attachment, and other processes against its property upon commencement of rehabilitation, subject only to the statutory exceptions. Creditors must present stayed claims in the centralized rehabilitation proceeding.

Application: The supplier seeks to enforce a precommencement monetary claim by seizing Meridian's own production equipment after receiving notice of the order. Earlier filing is not a statutory exception, and removing machinery needed for operations would defeat the asset-preservation purpose of the rehabilitation process.

Conclusion: Thus, levy and execution must stop, and the supplier must present its claim in rehabilitation, because the commencement order stays enforcement and no statutory exception applies.

rows.title: Presumption of Carrier Negligence for Damaged Cargo
rows.prompt: A shipper delivered sealed cartons of medical glass to Ocean Crest Lines in sound condition, as shown by a clean bill of lading and loading photographs. At destination, many cartons were crushed and wet. The carrier offered no loading plan, stowage record, weather log, or witness explaining the damage and merely referred to ordinary sea risks. Does proof of good delivery and damaged arrival create a rebuttable presumption that the common carrier was negligent?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The unexplained damage after receipt in good order raises the statutory presumption against the common carrier.

Legal Basis: Articles 1733 to 1735 of the Civil Code require common carriers to exercise extraordinary diligence over goods. Once the shipper proves delivery to the carrier in good condition and loss or damage before proper delivery, fault or negligence is presumed; the carrier must then prove an enumerated exempt cause and the diligence required by law.

Application: The clean bill of lading and photographs established that the medical glass entered Ocean Crest's custody undamaged, while destination inspection showed crushing and water exposure. Ocean Crest identified no specific exempt cause and produced no handling or voyage evidence capable of proving extraordinary diligence.

Conclusion: Hence, the unrebutted presumption of carrier negligence applies to the damaged cargo.

rows.title: Unauthorized Mortgage of Conjugal Property
rows.prompt: During marriage, Arman mortgaged two conjugal lots to secure his personal business loan by forging Belle's signature. The lender noticed that the identification photograph did not match the woman presented as Belle, yet made no inquiry. Belle rejected the mortgage immediately upon discovery and never later accepted it. Is the mortgage enforceable against the conjugal lots?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The mortgage is void as an encumbrance of the conjugal lots.

Legal Basis: Under Article 124 of the Family Code, one spouse may not dispose of or encumber conjugal property without the other spouse's written consent or court authority. Application: Belle gave no written consent because her signature was forged, and no court authorized the mortgage. Her immediate objection and complete nonacceptance also prevent the void transaction from becoming effective as a later accepted offer.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the mortgage is unenforceable against the conjugal lots because Belle gave no written consent, no court authorized the encumbrance, and she never accepted it.

rows.title: Foreign Spouse's Personality to Seek Nullity of a Philippine Marriage
rows.prompt: Paul, an American citizen, married Louella, a Filipina, in Manila. He later petitioned a Philippine court to declare their marriage void under Article 36, but the trial court dismissed solely because his foreign citizenship supposedly placed his family status beyond Philippine law. Does Paul have legal personality to petition for nullity of his own Philippine marriage?

Answer: Yes. Paul has legal personality to bring the petition.

Legal Basis: The rule governing declarations of absolute nullity authorizes either the husband or the wife to file the petition and makes no citizenship distinction. Conclusion: Wherefore, as a spouse directly affected by the Philippine marriage, Paul may petition for its declaration of nullity.

rows.title: Effect of a Co-owner's Sale of the Entire Property
rows.prompt: Ada, Ben, and Cora own an unpartitioned farm in equal shares. Without authority from the others, Ben sold the entire farm to Victor, who knew the title named all three co-owners. Ada argues that Ben's lack of authority makes the sale void even as to Ben's own share. Is Ada correct that the sale is entirely void?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The sale remains effective as to Ben's undivided share.

Legal Basis: Article 493 permits each co-owner to alienate, assign, or mortgage the co-owner's undivided interest even before partition. Application: Ben lacked power to transfer Ada's and Cora's interests, and Victor knew the farm was co-owned. Ben nevertheless owned an undivided one-third interest that Article 493 allowed him to alienate, subject to partition.

Conclusion: Wherefore, Victor acquired only Ben's undivided one-third interest, so the sale is not wholly void.

rows.title: Full Payment as a Suspensive Condition in a Contract to Sell
rows.prompt: Orchid Logistics agreed to buy a warehouse under a contract to sell that expressly retained title in the owner and required full payment before execution of an absolute deed. Application: The agreement retained title and made execution of the absolute deed dependent on complete payment. Orchid's unpaid balance meant the suspensive condition failed, so the owner's duty to transfer ownership never became effective.

Conclusion: Hence, the owner may refuse conveyance without first obtaining Article 1191 rescission because Orchid’s failure to pay the balance prevented the full-payment suspensive condition from occurring.

rows.title: Disinheritance Requires an Exclusive Statutory Cause
rows.prompt: A parent's will disinherits a child solely because the child married a person whom the parent considered irresponsible and disrespectful. Is the disinheritance valid without facts bringing the child's own conduct within an exclusive statutory cause?

Answer: No. Disinheritance is invalid without a cause expressly and exclusively provided by law.

Legal Basis: Articles 915 and 916 of the Civil Code require disinheritance to be made in a will and for a cause expressly specified by law. Application: Disapproval of the child's spouse and the spouse's behavior are not, without more, statutory acts of the child under Article 919. Strict compliance cannot be replaced by a generalized family grievance.

Conclusion: Thus, the disinheritance is ineffective and the child may protect the legitime.

rows.title: Mutuality and a Lender's Unilateral Interest-rate Reset
rows.prompt: A loan fixed nine percent interest for one year, then allowed Harbor Bank to impose any replacement rate it chose whenever it considered market conditions unfavorable. Answer: No. The unilateral reset violates the mutuality of contracts.

Legal Basis: Article 1308 requires a contract to bind both parties and prohibits leaving its validity or compliance to the will of only one party. Application: Harbor Bank alone determined when conditions were unfavorable and what replacement rate would apply. The contract supplied no external index, reciprocal choice, or later assent by Celso to the twenty-two percent figure.

Conclusion: Thus, the bank's unilaterally selected twenty-two percent rate is unenforceable for lack of mutuality.

rows.title: Annulment Does Not Automatically Alter a Child's Civil Status

Application: The child was born during the subsisting marriage and before the annulment judgment. Annulment and a private DNA test do not substitute for the exclusive, timely action required to impugn legitimacy.

rows.title: Employer Liability for an Employee's Quasi-delict
rows.prompt: ParcelHub instructed employee Tomas to drive its van to collect contracts from a client. After a five-minute pharmacy stop along the assigned route, Tomas resumed the business trip and injured a pedestrian while speeding. Legal Basis: Article 2180 makes an employer responsible for an employee's quasi-delict committed within the scope of assigned tasks. Application: Tomas had resumed the direct client trip in ParcelHub's van when the collision occurred, so the brief pharmacy stop did not remove him from the assigned task. A license and written rule alone do not prove careful selection and effective supervision.

Conclusion: Thus, ParcelHub is vicariously liable because Tomas was acting within his assigned business task when the injury occurred and ParcelHub failed to prove the statutory diligence defense.

rows.syllabus_topic: Special Contracts — Fiduciary Duty Concerning the Principal's Property
rows.title: Agent's Prohibition Against Acquiring an Adverse Title
rows.prompt: The Tad-y spouses authorized PNB under their mortgage to advance real-property taxes and act to protect the mortgaged lots. When the lots were sold for tax delinquency, PNB bought them at auction, later accepted full payment of the spouses' loans without foreclosure, and then claimed the lots as its own. May PNB retain a title acquired adversely to the spouses while acting within that agency?

rows.title: Good Faith Required for Priority in a Double Sale
rows.prompt: Sylvia first sold a titled farm to Leon, who immediately possessed, fenced, improved, and posted an ownership sign on it but did not register. Sylvia later sold the same farm to Nestor. Before paying and registering, Nestor saw Leon's open possession and sign but made no inquiry because Sylvia's certificate appeared clean. Does Nestor's earlier registration give him the better right under Article 1544?

Answer: No. Nestor's registration was not made in good faith.

Conclusion: Hence, Nestor's bad-faith registration cannot defeat Leon's earlier purchase and good-faith possession.

Conclusion: Thus, the supplier must return the mistaken payment under solutio indebiti.

rows.title: Unproved Foreign Law and Processual Presumption
rows.prompt: A Philippine-centered construction contract selects Singapore law, but the party invoking a foreign rule submits only counsel's memorandum and no competent proof of that law. May the unproved foreign rule displace Philippine law?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Unproved foreign law cannot displace Philippine law on the present record.

Legal Basis: Philippine Export and Foreign Loan Guarantee Corp. v. V.P. Eusebio and Saudi Arabian Airlines v. Rebesencio recognize party autonomy subject to substantial relationship, reasonable basis, mandatory law, and public policy. Unproved foreign law is presumed the same as Philippine law.

Application: Counsel's memorandum does not prove Singapore law. The project and performance are Philippine-centered, and no substantial foreign connection justifies displacing local protections.

Conclusion: Thus, the dispute should be decided under Philippine law on the present evidence.

rows.prompt: Three overseas nursing aides claimed underpayment under their approved contracts. rows.title: Abandonment Requires a Clear Intent to Sever Employment
rows.prompt: A restaurant worker reported for his usual shift but was denied entry and removed from the schedule. Within five days, he filed an illegal-dismissal complaint asking for reinstatement. Application: The worker attempted to report but the restaurant barred him and removed his schedule. His complaint followed within five days and expressly sought reinstatement, while the restaurant proved no communication or conduct showing a desire to quit.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the evidence shows exclusion from work and a wish to return, not abandonment.

rows.title: CBA Benefit Limited to the Defined Bargaining Unit
rows.prompt: A CBA grants the regular rank-and-file bargaining unit an eighteen percent share of the cooperative's net surplus. The cooperative separately promised the same percentage to managers, supervisors, and confidential employees, then charged those payments against the CBA pool and reduced the rank-and-file allocation. May the cooperative dilute the bargained share by including employees excluded from the CBA's defined unit?

Answer: No. The cooperative may not dilute the bargaining unit's share.

Legal Basis: A collective bargaining agreement is the law between the parties and must be read as a whole and performed in good faith. Application: The CBA expressly covers regular rank-and-file employees, while managers, supervisors, and confidential employees fall outside that unit. Debiting their separate grants from the same pool reduces the precise eighteen percent benefit the union negotiated.

Conclusion: Hence, the cooperative may not dilute the bargained share because the CBA assigns the eighteen-percent benefit exclusively to the defined rank-and-file bargaining unit.

rows.title: Employer Interference with the Right to Self-organization
rows.prompt: After AIM faculty members registered a labor organization, management categorically refused to recognize it, reduced a leader's teaching load, denied another organizer's scholarship because she signed the registration papers, and withheld a promotion after referring to the applicant's union activity. Does the totality of AIM's conduct constitute unfair labor practice by interference with self-organization?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The coordinated anti-union conduct constitutes unfair labor practice.

Legal Basis: Article 259(a) makes it employer unfair labor practice to interfere with, restrain, or coerce employees in exercising the right to self-organization. Acts facially within management prerogative lose that protection when, viewed in their totality with preceding and subsequent circumstances, substantial evidence shows that anti-union purpose motivated discrimination or disadvantage.

rows.title: Constructive Dismissal Through a Bad-faith Demotion and Transfer

rows.title: Labor-Tribunal Jurisdiction Over an Employment Training Bond

rows.title: Ordinary Member's Peaceful Participation in an Illegal Strike
rows.prompt: A final judgment declared a union strike illegal for statutory noncompliance. Nestor, an ordinary union member, peacefully joined the picket line but committed no violence, coercion, obstruction, or property damage. His employer dismissed him solely because he participated in the illegal strike, without alleging any individual illegal act. Was Nestor's dismissal valid?

Legal Basis: An ordinary union member does not lose employment merely by joining a strike later declared illegal. Conclusion: Hence, Nestor's dismissal based solely on peaceful participation in the illegal strike is invalid.

rows.title: Employer Verification Before Union-security Dismissal

rows.title: Separate Liability for Illegal Recruitment and Estafa
rows.prompt: Unlicensed Mira promised Carlo an overseas hotel job, displayed fabricated employer emails, and collected PHP 90,000 in placement fees, although she submitted no application and spent the money. Conclusion: Hence, upon proof of every element, Mira may be convicted of both illegal recruitment and estafa because each offense contains an element the other does not and neither absorbs the other.

rows.title: Control Test for an Employer-Employee Relationship
rows.prompt: Licensed physiotherapist Carina rents a room from a wellness center, chooses her patients and schedule, fixes her professional fees, and decides each treatment method. Legal Basis: Under the control test, an employer-employee relationship exists when the putative employer reserves the right to control not merely the desired result but also the means and methods by which the work is performed. Application: Carina alone selects patients, sets her schedule and fees, and determines how therapy is performed. The center's hours, sanitation, safety, dress, and advertising rules regulate the facility and presentation, not her therapeutic means or methods.

Conclusion: Thus, the center's neutral facility rules do not satisfy the control test for employment.

rows.title: Termination of a Probationary Employee for Unmet Disclosed Standards
rows.prompt: Clinic Orenda hired therapist Mae for six months and gave her signed copies of reasonable patient-safety and documentation standards on her first day. Before the probationary period expired, Orenda served written notice terminating her solely for failure to qualify, without using the twin-notice procedure for a disciplinary offense. Legal Basis: A probationary employee may be terminated for failure to meet reasonable qualification standards made known at the time of engagement. rows.title: Equal Pay for Substantially Equal Work
rows.prompt: A private school pays locally hired teachers lower base salaries than foreign-hired teachers. Both groups teach identical subjects, possess comparable licenses and experience, carry the same loads, and work under the same conditions. The school relies only on nationality and recruitment origin, while reimbursing documented relocation costs separately. Is the base-salary classification valid?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The nationality-based base-pay distinction is invalid.

Legal Basis: Employees who perform substantially equal work under similar conditions and possess comparable qualifications, skill, effort, and responsibility must receive equal pay unless the employer proves a real and job-related distinction. Nationality or foreign-hire status alone cannot justify lower compensation for equivalent work, although actual relocation costs may be separately reimbursed.

Application: The local and foreign-hired teachers have comparable credentials, assignments, responsibilities, evaluations, and working conditions. Separate relocation reimbursement addresses the foreign hires' documented expense and supplies no job-related basis for a permanent difference in base salary.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the base-salary classification is invalid because the two teacher groups perform substantially equal work under the same conditions and the school proved no job-related distinction.

rows.syllabus_topic: Felonies and Criminal Liability: RPC Book 1 and Related Laws — conspiracy as a mode of liability
rows.title: Conspiracy - Overt Acts Showing Conscious Concurrence
rows.prompt: Tomas attended a robbery planning meeting, drove the armed robbers to the warehouse, waited at the agreed escape point with the engine running, and warned them when guards approached. Messages assigned him the driver and lookout roles, but he never entered the warehouse or touched the stolen cargo. Can Tomas be held liable as a principal by conspiracy despite remaining outside?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Tomas may be held liable as a principal by conspiracy.

Legal Basis: Conspiracy requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of a common criminal design and the accused's conscious concurrence in it. Agreement may be inferred from coordinated overt acts before, during, and after the offense. Once conspiracy is established, the act of one conspirator in furtherance of the plan is attributable to all, even if a particular conspirator did not personally perform every element.

Application: Tomas joined the planning, transported the armed participants, occupied the assigned getaway position, and warned them of approaching guards. Those deliberate and coordinated acts advanced the known robbery plan and go far beyond mere presence or association. Personal entry into the warehouse was therefore unnecessary.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the robbery acts committed in furtherance of the conspiracy are attributable to Tomas as a principal.

rows.title: Self-Defense - Cessation of Unlawful Aggression
rows.prompt: An attacker struck Yuri once with a bottle, then dropped it, raised both empty hands, and backed across the street. Nearly a minute later, without any renewed threat, Yuri took a metal bar, chased the attacker, and broke his arm. Yuri invokes self-defense based on the earlier bottle strike. Was unlawful aggression still present when Yuri used the metal bar?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Unlawful aggression had already ceased.

Legal Basis: Unlawful aggression is the indispensable element of complete or incomplete self-defense. It must be an actual physical assault or an imminent and real threat at the moment defensive force is used. Once the aggressor has disarmed, withdrawn, and no longer presents an actual or imminent danger, later violence is retaliation rather than self-defense.

Application: The attacker dropped the bottle, displayed empty hands, and retreated across the street. Yuri waited nearly a minute, armed himself, and pursued despite the absence of a renewed threat. His later use of force answered a past attack, not an existing or imminent aggression.

Conclusion: Hence, Yuri cannot invoke self-defense for the chase and beating after the danger ended.

rows.syllabus_topic: Felonies and Criminal Liability: RPC Book 1 and Related Laws — Extinction of criminal liability by death before final judgment
rows.title: Death of the Accused Pending Appeal
rows.prompt: An accused dies while the conviction is still under appeal and before final judgment. Must the criminal case and civil liability based solely on the offense be extinguished, without prejudice to independently sourced civil claims?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Death before final judgment extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto.

Legal Basis: Article 89(1) of the Revised Penal Code extinguishes criminal liability by death before final judgment. People v. Brillantes, applying People v. Application: Because the conviction remained on appeal, it had not become final when the accused died. No criminal penalty may be imposed, while a civil claim based on another source of obligation may proceed separately if legally available.

Conclusion: Thus, the appeal and criminal case must be dismissed, subject to the stated civil-law qualification.

rows.title: Natural Consequences and Proximate Cause Under Article 4
rows.prompt: During an intentional unlawful assault, Diego chases the victim onto an elevated footbridge. The victim reasonably flees, falls, and dies; no independent event intervenes. Is Diego criminally liable for the death even though he intended only to injure?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Diego is liable for the natural and proximate consequence of his intentional felony.

Legal Basis: Article 4 of the Revised Penal Code makes one who commits an intentional felony liable for all its natural and logical consequences. Talampas v. People requires a causal chain unbroken by an efficient intervening cause.

Application: The fatal fall was a foreseeable and immediate response to Diego's unlawful pursuit. Because no independent superseding cause broke the chain, the resulting death is attributable to the original felony.

Conclusion: Thus, the offender answers for the death notwithstanding that the resulting harm exceeded his specific intent.

rows.title: Impossible Crime - Absent Victim
rows.prompt: Olive entered a vacant cottage believing Quinn was behind a curtain and fired twice at a lifelike mannequin with intent to kill. Quinn had left hours earlier. The firearm was capable, but no living victim was present, and the facts exclude any other punishable offense. Is Olive liable for attempted homicide?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Olive is not liable for attempted homicide on the stated facts.

Legal Basis: An impossible crime exists when a person acts with evil intent against persons or property, accomplishment is inherently impossible or the means are inadequate or ineffectual, and the act does not constitute another violation of the Revised Penal Code. Attempted homicide instead requires an existing victim against whom overt acts can directly commence an executable killing.

Application: Olive had genuine homicidal intent and used a capable weapon, but Quinn was absent before the shooting began. The intended killing was factually impossible at the time of the acts because no living victim was exposed. The problem also removes any independent offense that would displace the impossible-crime provision.

Conclusion: Hence, Olive is liable for an impossible crime rather than attempted homicide because no living victim existed when she fired.

rows.title: Compound Complex Crime - One Grenade, Multiple Felonies
rows.prompt: Lando intentionally threw one grenade into a room occupied by four rivals. The single explosion killed one and inflicted ordinarily fatal wounds on the other three, who survived because of surgery. Forensic evidence attributes every injury to that one detonation. Should the resulting grave felonies be treated as one compound complex crime under Article 48?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The resulting grave felonies should be treated as one compound complex crime.

Legal Basis: Article 48 applies when one physical act produces two or more grave or less grave felonies. The law treats the offenses as a compound complex crime and imposes the penalty for the most serious offense in its maximum period. The rule does not merge light felonies and does not apply when separate volitional acts produce the offenses.

Application: Lando performed one physical act by throwing the single grenade, and that one detonation caused one death and three ordinarily fatal wounds. Because timely surgery alone prevented the other deaths, the homicide and three frustrated homicides all arose from the same act.

Conclusion: Wherefore, Article 48 governs the grave felonies produced by the single explosion.

Conclusion: Thus, the prosecution should charge rebellion, with the furthering acts absorbed on the stated facts.

rows.title: Graft - Procurement Irregularity Does Not Prove Undue Injury
rows.prompt: Municipal officials used donated funds to complete a public pathway and gym without public bidding, and some audit documents remained missing. The prosecution presented no reference price showing that bidding would have reduced the cost and no other proof of pecuniary loss to the municipality. Is a conviction under the undue-injury mode of Section 3(e) of R.A. No. 3019 valid solely because of those procurement and documentation defects?

Conclusion: Thus, the officials cannot be convicted under the undue-injury mode on those irregularities alone.

rows.title: Cyberlibel - Publication Through a Computer System
rows.prompt: Ysolde knowingly uploaded a public post falsely accusing the named Zeno of theft. Numerous readers viewed and shared it. The prosecution proved defamatory imputation, identification, publication, malice, and Ysolde's authorship through the platform records. Ysolde argues that libel requires a printed paper and that an online post cannot satisfy publication. Can the public online post constitute cyberlibel?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. The public online post can constitute cyberlibel.

Legal Basis: Cyberlibel consists of libel committed through a computer system or a similar future means. The prosecution must prove every element of libel, including defamatory imputation, publication to a third person, identification, and the required malice, together with the accused's own use of the computer system. Publication is communication to a third person and is not limited to paper.

Application: Ysolde authored and uploaded the defamatory accusation on a publicly accessible platform, where third persons viewed and redistributed it. The post named Zeno, and the remaining libel elements and Ysolde's authorship were proved. Digital transmission therefore supplies the computer-system mode and the required publication.

Conclusion: Thus, Ysolde may be held liable for cyberlibel because her public computer-system post communicated the defamatory accusation to third persons, satisfying publication without a paper medium.

rows.title: Qualified Trafficking - Minor Victim's Consent

Answer: Yes. The pastor is liable for qualified trafficking on the stated facts.

Because the victims were children and forced-labor exploitation was proved, their agreement to remain at the school and their asserted religious motivation cannot excuse or mitigate the trafficking.

Conclusion: Hence, the pastor may be convicted of qualified trafficking because the victims were minors, whose consent is immaterial, and the proven recruitment and forced-labor exploitation satisfy the child-trafficking rule.

rows.title: Drug Plea Bargaining - Individualized Judicial Review

The trial judge approved it without receiving evidence or making findings on recidivism, habituality, repeated charges, relapse after rehabilitation, or the strength of the prosecution evidence. Did the judge properly approve the plea without assessing those circumstances?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The judge did not properly approve the plea without the required assessment.

Legal Basis: A drug-case plea proposal that falls within the Supreme Court's framework is not automatically acceptable. Application: The judge accepted the proposed plea without evidence or findings on any listed disqualifier and without evaluating the strength of the prosecution case. The record therefore shows no individualized exercise of the judicial discretion required by the framework.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the plea must be reconsidered after the trial court conducts the required assessment.

Conclusion: Thus, the absence of proven pecuniary damage does not defeat the falsification charge.

rows.title: Plunder - Combination or Series of Overt Acts
rows.prompt: A public officer accepted one unlawful payment of PHP 55 million in a single completed transfer. The Information alleges no second predicate act, no connected transaction, and no additional method of acquiring ill-gotten wealth, but calls the amount an overall pattern of plunder. Does the one payment satisfy the combination-or-series element of plunder?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. One payment does not satisfy the combination-or-series element.

Legal Basis: Plunder requires ill-gotten wealth reaching the statutory threshold to be amassed through a combination or series of overt criminal acts forming an overall pattern. A series requires at least two acts of the same statutory category, while a combination requires at least two acts from different categories; the amount threshold cannot substitute for that required plurality.

Application: The prosecution proved only one PHP 55 million payment in one completed transfer and alleged no second predicate act, connected transaction, or different acquisition method. Although the amount exceeds the threshold, the single transaction cannot form either a series or a combination.

Conclusion: Wherefore, the plunder charge is deficient because one transfer, regardless of amount, cannot establish the statutorily required combination or series of overt acts.

rows.title: Fencing - Knowledge from Circumstances
rows.prompt: Uriah, an experienced second-hand electronics dealer, bought five laptops from a stranger for one-fourth of their market value. School labels had been scraped off, and he requested no receipt or identification before advertising the units for profit. The laptops were proved stolen, although the principal thief had not been convicted. Can Uriah be convicted of fencing without a prior conviction of the thief?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: Yes. Uriah can be convicted of fencing without a prior conviction of the thief.

Legal Basis: A prior conviction of the principal thief is not an element of fencing. The prosecution may independently prove that the property came from robbery or theft and that the accused dealt in it with the knowledge required by P.D. No. 1612.

Application: The laptops were independently proved stolen, and Uriah's experience, the one-fourth price, the scraped school labels, his failure to obtain a receipt or seller identification, and his resale advertisement supplied proof of knowledgeable dealing. Because those facts establish the antecedent theft and Uriah's conduct without relying on a judgment against the thief, the absence of the thief's conviction does not bar fencing liability.

Conclusion: Wherefore, Uriah may be convicted of fencing without the thief's prior conviction because that conviction is not an element and the antecedent theft may be proved independently.

Conclusion: Thus, the breakup does not defeat the VAWC charge because R.A. No. 9262 expressly covers violence by a person with whom the victim had a dating relationship.

rows.title: Theft - No Frustrated Stage
rows.prompt: Berto removed a sealed camera from a shop display, concealed it in his backpack, and exercised exclusive control over it before staff stopped him near the exit. rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The theft was not merely frustrated; it was consummated.

Legal Basis: Theft is consummated when personal property is taken without the owner's consent, with intent to gain, and without violence, intimidation, or force upon things. Conclusion: Hence, Berto committed consummated theft because concealment placed the camera under his possession and control, completing the taking without any need to leave the store or freely dispose of it.

rows.syllabus_topic: Fundamental Principles — intent and voluntariness
rows.title: Mala Prohibita - Voluntary Prohibited Act
rows.prompt: After receiving a regulator's written instruction that registration was required, Nara personally approved and sold unregistered pooled-investment notes. She admits the voluntary sales but says she honestly believed sophisticated buyers did not need protection. The charged regulatory offense does not make fraud an element. Does Nara's good-faith disagreement by itself negate criminal liability?

Answer: No. Her good-faith disagreement does not by itself negate liability.

Legal Basis: For a malum prohibitum offense, the prosecution ordinarily need not prove criminal intent or a fraudulent motive when the statute punishes the prohibited act itself. It must still prove a conscious and voluntary act, the accused's participation, and every element specified by the law. Application: Nara received actual notice of the registration requirement and then personally authorized the offers and accepted subscription money. Those facts prove conscious and voluntary participation. Because fraud is not an element of the charged regulatory offense, her belief about buyer sophistication does not erase the prohibited sales.

Conclusion: Thus, good-faith disagreement is not a defense once the voluntary statutory violation and all remaining elements are proved.

rows.syllabus_topic: Civil Procedure — judicial review of CIAC arbitral awards
rows.title: CIAC Awards - Limited Factual Review Under Rule 65
rows.prompt: A CIAC tribunal awarded a contractor compensation after hearings in which both parties presented evidence. The owner filed a Rule 65 petition in the Court of Appeals and sought reweighing of the evidence because it disagreed with the tribunal's evidentiary rulings and valuation of retained equipment. The record shows no corruption, fraud, misconduct, evident partiality, incapacity, excess of powers, or illegal arbitral process. May the Court of Appeals reexamine the factual merits on those grounds?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The Court of Appeals may not reexamine the factual merits on those grounds.

Legal Basis: Factual review of a CIAC award in the Court of Appeals through Rule 65 is confined to a sufficient and demonstrable challenge to the tribunal's integrity or to unconstitutional or illegal conduct of the arbitral process. Mere disagreement with factual findings, evidentiary rulings, or valuation does not open the award to merits review.

Application: The owner identifies only adverse evidentiary rulings and disagreement with the equipment valuation after both parties were heard. Because the facts disclose none of the limited integrity or legality grounds, the Rule 65 petition cannot support a fresh weighing of the arbitral record.

Conclusion: Thus, the Court of Appeals must respect the CIAC findings because the owner showed no corruption, fraud, partiality, excess of authority, or illegality in the arbitral process to justify Rule 65 factual review.

rows.syllabus_topic: Civil Procedure — service of judgments by registered mail
rows.title: Registered Mail - Proof of Service of Judgment
rows.prompt: A municipal officer appealed after actually learning of an adverse disciplinary decision through a later audit notice. The agency claimed earlier service based only on a registry return card marked refused to accept, but the card did not identify who refused and no detailed postmaster certification established how, when, or upon whom delivery was attempted. Official municipal files contained no copy of the decision. Did the bare registry return card prove the earlier service?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The bare registry return card did not prove the earlier service.

Legal Basis: When service of a judgment by registered mail is disputed, a registry return card bearing an unidentified refusal notation does not by itself prove service. Competent proof must establish when, how, and upon whom delivery was attempted.

Application: The return card stated only refused to accept, without identifying the person who refused or the circumstances of the attempted delivery. No detailed postmaster certification or copy in the municipal files corroborated earlier service, so the agency did not prove that the officer was served before the later audit notice.

Conclusion: Hence, the appeal cannot be treated as late because the unidentified refusal notation and unsupported return card did not competently prove earlier service of the decision.

rows.syllabus_topic: Civil Procedure — bar by prior judgment
rows.title: Res Judicata - Relabeling the Same Cause
rows.prompt: Iris lost a final ownership action against Jomar after a full trial in a court with jurisdiction. She later sued Jomar over the same parcel, relied on the same deed, and again sought a declaration of ownership, but placed a different legal label on the complaint. Is the second action barred by prior judgment despite the changed label?

Answer: Yes. The second action is barred by prior judgment.

Legal Basis: Bar by prior judgment applies when a court with jurisdiction rendered a final judgment on the merits and the later action presents identity of parties, subject matter, and causes of action. Application: The earlier judgment was final and followed a full trial before a competent court. Both suits involve Iris and Jomar, the same parcel, the same deed, and the same claimed ownership. The new label does not alter the operative facts or requested declaration.

Conclusion: Thus, the court should dismiss the second ownership action because the final prior judgment involved the same parties, parcel, deed, operative facts, and requested ownership relief.

rows.syllabus_topic: Legal and Judicial Ethics — CPRA Canon III, Section 13
rows.title: Conflict of Interest - Directly Adverse Concurrent Representation
rows.prompt: Attorney Mira represents Aurora in defending its registered title to a garden. While that engagement remains active, Mira accepts another group as a client and signs its complaint to cancel Aurora's title over the same land. She orally discloses the dual representation but neither explains the material risks nor obtains written informed consent from every concerned client. Did Mira violate the CPRA rule on conflict of interest?

Answer: Yes. Mira violated the conflict-of-interest rule.

Legal Basis: Canon III, Section 13 of the CPRA prohibits representation of conflicting interests unless every concerned client gives written informed consent after full disclosure of the facts and material risks. A conflict exists when advancing one client's claim requires the lawyer to oppose a position the lawyer must protect for another current client.

Application: Mira owed Aurora a continuing duty to defend its title, yet she signed the second client's complaint attacking that same title. Success for either client would defeat the other, and Mira obtained only oral disclosure without explaining the material risks or securing the required written consent.

Conclusion: Thus, Mira's directly adverse concurrent representation violated the CPRA.

rows.syllabus_topic: Evidence — authentication of private electronic documents
rows.title: Electronic Evidence - Duplicate Rule Does Not Prove Authenticity
rows.prompt: A supplier offers a printed copy of an email accepting a PHP 6 million proposal. The alleged sender denies authorship, several employees shared the displayed account, and the supplier presents no recipient testimony, metadata, server log, digital signature, security procedure, or other attribution evidence. The supplier relies only on the rule allowing electronic duplicates. Is the email admissible solely because the copy may qualify as a duplicate?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. Duplicate status alone does not make the disputed email admissible.

Legal Basis: A disputed private electronic document must be authenticated by evidence showing that it is what the proponent claims, such as testimony, metadata, a digital signature, a security procedure, or reliable system and attribution proof. The electronic-duplicate rule concerns the form of an otherwise authenticated record and does not dispense with authenticity.

Application: The alleged sender denied authorship, and multiple employees could use the same account. Without recipient testimony, metadata, logs, signature, security procedure, or comparable linking proof, the printout remains unattributed. Calling it a duplicate answers only its form and leaves authenticity unproved.

Conclusion: Thus, the supplier must authenticate the email before it may be admitted.

rows.syllabus_topic: Evidence — Hearsay definition and truth-of-the-assertion purpose
rows.title: Dispatcher's Out-of-Court Statement Offered for Its Truth
rows.prompt: A passenger sues a bus company after a collision. To prove defective brakes, the passenger calls a bystander who says the dispatcher told him before the trip that the brakes had failed inspection. The dispatcher does not testify, and no hearsay exclusion or exception is established. Is the bystander's testimony admissible to prove that the brakes were defective?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The dispatcher's out-of-court assertion is inadmissible hearsay when offered for its truth.

Legal Basis: Under Rule 130, hearsay is an out-of-court statement offered to prove the truth of what it asserts and is inadmissible unless a rule excludes it from hearsay or supplies an exception. A nontruth purpose must be genuinely relevant and cannot be used as a pretext.

Application: The bystander has no personal knowledge of the brake condition. The passenger offers the dispatcher's statement precisely to prove defective brakes, and the facts establish no applicable exclusion or exception.

Conclusion: Thus, the testimony must be excluded when offered to prove the asserted brake defect.

rows.title: Information - Allegations for the Attempted Stage
rows.prompt: An Information for attempted homicide alleges the date and place and states that Alex, with intent to kill, thrust a knife toward Ben's chest but did not kill him. It does not allege that Alex failed to perform all acts of execution because of a cause or accident other than his spontaneous desistance. Is the Information sufficient to charge the attempted stage?
rows.suggested_answer:
Answer: No. The Information does not sufficiently allege the attempted stage.

Legal Basis: Rule 110 requires an Information to state the acts or omissions constituting every essential element of the charged offense. Under Article 6, an attempted felony requires direct commencement by overt acts and nonperformance of all acts of execution because of a cause or accident other than the offender's spontaneous desistance.

Application: The Information alleges homicidal intent and a knife thrust but says only that Ben was not killed. It omits the indispensable circumstance explaining that Alex failed to complete the acts of execution because of an independent cause rather than a voluntary abandonment.

Conclusion: Hence, the Information is insufficient because it omitted the essential allegation that noncompletion resulted from a cause other than Alex's spontaneous desistance.
